intro: The biggest story in AI today is one person walking out the door — and the earthquake it's causing. David Robinson, who literally wrote OpenAI's safety reports, resigned this week calling the company's culture "broken," adding fuel to a growing exodus of safety researchers sounding alarms about how fast the industry is moving. Beyond the safety debate, today's digest covers Amazon playing defense on data centers, Capcom's vision for AI-assisted game development, and a new wave of AI agents that live right in your text messages.

stories.title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’
stories.summary: David Robinson, a safety leader at OpenAI who led the writing of safety reports for the company's product releases, has resigned. In an essay titled 'I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken,' he warned that AI companies are not being careful enough in developing the technology. He joins a growing list of insiders who have urged the industry to exercise greater caution with rapidly advancing AI.
stories.opinion: The continued departure of safety-focused personnel from leading AI companies is a significant signal worth paying attention to. When people whose specific job is to evaluate risk decide the organization isn't taking that risk seriously enough, it carries more weight than outside criticism. Whether or not one agrees with any particular departing researcher's assessment, the pattern itself — multiple safety-oriented employees leaving and speaking publicly — suggests a real cultural tension betwe…

stories.title: Amazon responds to data center backlash, says it no longer uses NDAs
stories.summary: Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman published a blog post responding to growing backlash against data centers across the United States. He announced that Amazon has stopped using nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) with government agencies when seeking data center permits, addressing a key transparency complaint from critics including activist Erin Brockovich. Garman pushed back against what he called four 'myths' about data centers — excessive water consumption, increased electricity costs, pollution, and lack of community benefits — citing Amazon's own data. However, the article notes counterpoints to each claim: scientists say independent study is needed since tech companies self-report usage data, an independent watchdog linked data centers to a 76% price increase on America's largest electrical grid, and a planned Amazon data center in Texas holds permits allowing more carbon dioxide e…
stories.opinion: Amazon's move to drop NDAs is a pragmatic concession to political reality rather than a genuine transparency initiative — the company is responding to the threat of over 100 moratoriums that could stall its infrastructure expansion. Garman's framing of data center concerns as 'myths' is undermined by his reliance on Amazon's own self-reported data, especially when independent researchers have explicitly called for third-party verification. The comparison of data center water usage to golf cours…

stories.title: Capcom is preparing for a ‘future where we create games together with AI’
stories.summary: Capcom is planning to incrementally integrate AI technology into its RE Engine game development workflows. During a presentation at Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026, programmer Satoshi Ishida outlined the company's vision to evolve the RE Engine into an 'AI-generation game engine,' working toward 'a future where we create games together with AI.' The company has previously stated it will not use AI-generated assets in its final games, instead focusing on using AI to improve development efficiency for large-scale projects like Resident Evil, where even simple tasks can be extremely time-consuming.
stories.opinion: Capcom's approach represents a pragmatic middle ground in the gaming industry's AI debate. By committing to not using AI-generated assets in finished products while embracing AI for workflow efficiency, they're trying to thread a needle between productivity gains and creative integrity. However, the language about building toward an 'AI-generation game engine' and creating games 'together with AI' is notably open-ended and could signal a gradual expansion of AI's role beyond just backend toolin…

stories.title: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’
stories.summary: David Robinson, a longtime OpenAI safety employee who led safety report writing for major product launches, has resigned and published an essay in The Atlantic claiming OpenAI's 'culture is broken.' With three-and-a-half years at the company, Robinson argues that OpenAI's 'iterative deployment' approach guarantees periodic failures whose scale grows with system capability. He pointed to recent incidents including a breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents and discoveries of rogue agents as evidence. Robinson called for frontier AI companies to operate more like nuclear power plants or airports with layers of redundancy, noting he never encountered colleagues with experience in such safety-critical industries. His resignation follows Jacob Coxon's departure from both OpenAI and Anthropic, which sparked broader industry debate and led to AI executives signing a non-binding safety p…
stories.opinion: Robinson's core argument — that Silicon Valley's 'move fast and break things' culture is fundamentally incompatible with developing potentially superintelligent systems — is compelling and not new, but gains weight through his insider perspective on how safety reports actually function at OpenAI. The comparison to nuclear power plants and aviation is apt in principle but may understate the difficulty: those industries developed safety cultures over decades of catastrophic failures, and AI devel…

stories.title: An OpenAI safety employee has quit and is sounding the alarm
stories.summary: David Robinson, who wrote safety reports for OpenAI's major model releases, resigned this week and published an editorial in The Atlantic warning that the AI industry's safety culture is 'fundamentally broken.' He argues the problem goes deeper than new rules or regulations — Silicon Valley's culture of 'extreme confidence,' 'perpetual sprints,' and 'unimpeded optimism' systematically ignores or underestimates risks. Robinson calls for AI companies to adopt 'nuclear-level safeguards,' comparing the needed rigor to running nuclear power plants or busy airports with layers of redundancy and careful planning. He joins a growing wave of safety researchers leaving major AI firms, following Jacob Coxon's departure from Anthropic.
stories.opinion: Robinson's nuclear-safeguard analogy is apt and his critique of Silicon Valley's cultural blind spots is well-founded — the move-fast-and-break-things ethos is genuinely dangerous when applied to systems with the potential impact of frontier AI models. However, there's a tension in these warnings: the people sounding the alarm helped build these systems and often stayed silent while employed, which undercuts urgency even if it doesn't invalidate the message. The more substantive question is whe…

stories.title: All the AI agents that can live in your text messages
stories.summary: TechCrunch highlights a growing category of AI agents that operate through text messaging (SMS, iMessage, RCS, WhatsApp, Telegram) rather than requiring dedicated apps. Notable examples include Caddy (an iMessage/RCS assistant that connects to calendars and conversations to identify actionable items), Fambot (a family-oriented 'chief of staff' that organizes school communications, sports, meal planning, and sends nightly summaries via SMS, with $3.5M in pre-seed funding), Folk (available across iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram with its own private cloud computer for multi-step tasks), and Instinct (the buzziest entry with a $10 billion valuation after a $1 billion funding round). These agents can schedule appointments, manage calendars, research trips, send emails, make reservations, shop online, and set reminders — all through conversational text interfaces users already know how to us…
stories.opinion: This trend represents a pragmatic UX insight: the best interface for an AI assistant might not be another app but the messaging layer people already live in. By meeting users in SMS, iMessage, or WhatsApp, these agents sidestep app fatigue and the cold-start problem that kills most new consumer apps. The real differentiator will be depth of integration and reliability of task execution — it's easy to demo an agent booking a restaurant, but hard to make it work consistently across thousands of e…
